title: More than 700,000 Russian troops died in the war in Ukraine by late September 2026, Meduza and Mediazona estimate — Meduza
html:
On November 1, news broke that hackers from the Belarusian Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow had breached the website of Rosstat, Russia’s federal statistics agency, and obtained data on Russian military losses in the war through fall 2026. The hackers used that data to produce their own estimate of how many Russians had been killed on the front lines. They also shared the database with reporters, including those at Meduza and Mediazona, which have been tracking Russia’s military death toll together for several years. We examined the hacked database and concluded that it was very likely authentic. We then compared its records with other sources and ran a new analysis. Our earlier studies relied mainly on data from the Register of Inheritance Cases. The Rosstat database makes the new estimate more reliable. Another important change: The new estimate counts both registered deaths and missing service members, many of whom will likely be confirmed dead.

Based on registered deaths alone, we estimate that 490,000 Russian service members had been killed by fall 2026. Including missing service members brings the estimate to more than 700,000.

Here’s how Meduza and Mediazona arrived at these grim estimates.

What to know about our new study

By the end of September 2026, at least 490,000 Russian service members had been killed in the war with Ukraine. These are people whose deaths have already been registered and appear in the leaked Rosstat documents. Meduza and Mediazona jointly checked the data obtained by the hackers and found it to be genuine. It would simply be impossible to fake this many records that match information from other sources.

The leak is valuable because it contains a large amount of previously unavailable data. It lets us recheck the estimates of Russian military losses that Meduza has calculated since 2023 based on the Register of Inheritance Cases. But the Rosstat documents alone can’t tell us how many people have died in the war. Even this database gives only a partial count of Russia’s military deaths. The database doesn’t include service members who have been killed but whose deaths haven’t yet been registered.

Both the leaked data and the inheritance register show that such registrations still happen, though rarely, even for deaths dating back to 2022 and 2023. Since 2024, the share of late registrations has grown dramatically, and it continues to rise. Today, it’s simply impossible to leave this category out of an overall estimate of the dead. But estimating how many deaths remain unregistered isn’t easy. Rosstat’s data alone isn’t enough, so additional sources are needed, and the analysis requires complex statistical methods.

Using all the information available to Meduza and Mediazona, we estimated the full death toll, including deaths that will be registered later. We did this using methods from actuarial science and epidemiology. Analysts in both fields calculate the number of events that have happened but haven’t yet shown up in the data, a problem similar to the one we face.

The final estimate is grim. We estimate that more than 700,000 Russian troops had been killed by the end of September 2026, compared with 490,000 registered deaths. Tests on older data showed that the estimate could be off by a wide margin, with nearly all the uncertainty concentrated in the most recent 12 months. The estimates for earlier years are considerably more precise and explicitly account for both recorded deaths and missing service members who have yet to appear in the death records.

This report is divided into three parts:

  • First, we’ll explain what’s in the leaked database and whether it can be trusted.
  • Then we’ll explain how we identified war deaths in the database.
  • Finally, we’ll explain how we estimated the actual death toll, including deaths that will be registered later.

And of course, we’ll discuss our previous calculations and show where we were wrong and where we were right.

For readers who want the short version, here are answers to some basic questions.

What is the Unified State Register of Civil Status Records (EGR ZAGS), the source of the leaked data?

It’s an information system through which civil registry offices exchange data on births, deaths, marriages, and divorces. The creation of the database was authorized in 2016 and it went into operation in October 2018. The system was developed by Russia’s Federal Tax Service. Rosstat received anonymized exports from it, and it was these copies that ended up in the hackers’ hands. So far, journalists have been given access only to the data on deaths, but the full archive also contains information on other civil status records.

What does the EGR ZAGS tell us about military deaths?

Rosstat’s copy of the system doesn’t include the names of the deceased, but it does contain plenty of other information that makes it possible to link records from different sources: dates of birth and death, the dates and numbers of registration records, and details of the registry offices themselves. It also contains information that no other source has made available until now: data from death certificates describing the causes of death, as well as the addresses where people died.

The causes of death in the EGR ZAGS can’t be fully trusted. In the past, especially at the peak of the coronavirus pandemic, medical workers often failed to list the correct causes, apparently because of outside pressure. So in addition to simply counting records with a “military” cause of death (listed for 425,000 unique deaths), we analyzed other fields in the database. We also calculated excess male mortality, a measure that does not depend on which deaths Rosstat classifies as military or nonmilitary.

The figures largely agreed, and the discrepancies have clear explanations.

Does the leak offer anything fundamentally new for understanding military deaths?

Not really. First, Rosstat had already published aggregated data on registered deaths through 2023, and researchers had already used it to calculate military deaths. The new figures add data for 2024, 2025, and part of 2026.

Second, for several years we’ve been estimating military losses using another large database that was available long before the current leak: the Register of Inheritance Cases. For periods far enough in the past, our estimates based on the inheritance register closely matched what the civil registry showed several years later. For more recent years, the figures differ substantially because both databases lack records of deaths that have yet to be registered. And the number of deaths registered after long delays keeps growing.

Can the civil and inheritance registers tell us how many troops have died recently if records take time to appear?

There are delays, but we now know how to deal with them. The key advance isn’t simply that we now have the civil registry data but that we can use it to estimate how many deaths local offices have recorded that have yet to appear in any database.

What data did the hackers obtain? And can the database be trusted?

The Belarusian Cyber Partisans and the Ukrainian hacker group Silent Crow jointly broke into Rosstat’s electronic document management system and obtained an archive of the agency’s data covering the last several years. Among other things, the hackers gave journalists unique, previously unavailable information on deaths in Russia during the war. They obtained the full set of detailed death records that Rosstat receives from the EGR ZAGS system. The archive contains information on almost all death registrations from the beginning of 2021 to the end of September 2026. It doesn’t include names, but it does have detailed data on causes of death and other information. The raw data also contains many duplicates and corrected entries, which made processing it no small task.

Below, we describe exactly how we processed this raw data. For those who aren’t interested in the details, here’s the answer up front: the EGR ZAGS records document 11,658,178 distinct deaths.

Here is how the source data is structured and how we processed it before analysis

The raw death data comes from three sources.

  • The first is a copy of Rosstat’s MongoDB database, called deathFacts, which stores anonymized death records. The hackers initially obtained it by breaking into Rosstat’s internal network. The data in it runs only through early August 2026.
  • The second is a separate export of records added to the same database while the hackers had access to the network. It includes only deaths through the end of August.
  • The third is a copy of the PostgreSQL database of the Interdepartmental Electronic Interaction System, or SMEV, which received death records until the hackers lost access at the end of September 2026.

Rosstat received already-anonymized “raw” records from EGR ZAGS through SMEV. The system was introduced in June 2023; before that, Rosstat apparently received the data each month in a separate table for each region. Once SMEV went into use, it automatically fed records into the agency’s internal database, and records underwent additional processing: some fields were discarded, and some empty ones were filled in. If SMEV left a dash where the exact day of death should be, Rosstat entered either the first of the month or the date on the civil death record.

In total, this amounts to 29.7 million records in MongoDB from 2021 through the end of August 2026 (the database holds only about 100,000 records for earlier years) and 15 million “raw” records from June 2023 through the end of September 2026.

Records do not equal unique deaths: almost every death has several versions. In most cases, later versions clarify information or fill in blanks, such as by specifying a cause of death or adding a previously unknown date. MongoDB has about 11.7 million unique numbers, and SMEV has 6.7 million.

We kept only the latest valid version, which was usually the most complete. Sometimes a record has no current version, and the last one is marked in the database as revoked; we found about 286,000 such cases. This usually means the death was entered into the database outside the “reporting period” and was not used in official statistics. In 23,000 cases, we were able to find a new record to replace the revoked one, based on dates of birth and death, place of birth, or the number on the document confirming the death. In the remaining 263,000 cases, we kept the revoked version as evidence of a unique death.

The records in the two databases overlap: SMEV adds about 210,000 new records and 60,000 new versions of records already in the database.

In principle, every death record should carry a unique number: a 21-digit code that follows a prescribed format. It begins with the “EGR section,” which is always 1 for records. The second digit indicates the type of record: birth, death, marriage, or divorce; for deaths it is always 7. The next three digits show the year of the record, the following eight identify the registry office or agency that issued it, and five more give the sequential number of that type of record at that office (the first death of the year at a given office, for example, would be recorded as 00001). The 19th and 20th digits represent an “additional marker,” and the 21st is a checksum.

“Additional markers” are needed to distinguish between two versions of the same record, for example when digitizing a paper version or when there is no access to the online records database. As a result, the same death can be registered with the same sequential number but a different 21-digit number, differing only in the last three digits: the additional marker and the checksum. We merged records with identical 18-digit segments where the dates of birth and death and sex matched, turning 375,000 records into 152,000 unique deaths (usually two or three versions of one death, and in one case four).

In practice, registry offices sometimes issue two original records (marked 00 in the additional-marker field) with the same sequential number. When one of these is entered into the online database, it may be assigned a different code, say 10. As a result, two different deaths end up sharing everything except the last three digits. In the Rosstat database, we found cases where different people were recorded under the same number in different versions of what was ostensibly the same record. In some cases we were able to find new records for these “overwritten” versions, but in about 1,000 cases we had to keep two different deaths under one record number.

We separately merged duplicates in cases where the same death was re-registered at a different registry office. This happened often with deaths originally registered at registry offices in the Rostov region, and with deaths declared by a court. In general, the dates of birth and death together are a fairly reliable way to identify a specific death. In most cases, each pair occurs once or twice, rarely as many as five times, and only in isolated cases more often, usually when the full date is unknown and is recorded as the first day of the month or year. Any additional matching indicator makes identification unambiguous: a matching place of birth, the number on the document confirming the death (allowing for a one-character typo), place of death, or name, if known. Many records are transferred to the “home” registry office serving the deceased person’s place of residence; in such cases, the record date is usually listed as the first day of the month, and the region on the death certificate matches the original region where the record was filed. The death certificate number alone is not unique and is used only together with other indicators. We used this approach to merge about 6,000 more records.

In the end, we arrived at 11,658,178 unique deaths. This count may still contain a small number of duplicates, for example when records are incomplete or contain errors, or it may count two deaths as one in rare cases when twins died at the same time and Rosstat has no information about the documents confirming their deaths.

We also had to make corrections and restore some data from the SMEV database that was missing from the Rosstat database. The first issue involves incomplete dates. For some deaths, Russian registries record only the month, or even just the year, of death. Rosstat filled in those records by entering the first of the month, or even January 1 of that year, as the date of death; we added notes about incomplete dates. In about 11,000 cases, the Rosstat database contained a note that the dates of birth and death had both been shifted by one year. We do not know why this was done, but we restored the original dates.
